newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. says Iraq shares in slowing oil-aid delivery.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Iraq shares in slowing oil-aid delivery.

text.p: The United States on Thursday said Iraq, not just the United Nations, was to blame for the slow pace of humanitarian aid deliveries under the oil-for-food deal.
U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson, seeking to deflect a constant stream of criticism from Baghdad that Washington was working to block aid shipments, said part of the blame must be put on Iraq.
"Not all the bureaucratic delays are here in New York, there are bureaucratic delays in Iraq," said Richardson, noting the plan's success depended on Iraq removing some of the bureaucratic obstacles.
Although Iraq has been contracting to sell oil since the plan's start on December 10, no food or supplies have yet arrived in Iraq for distribution.
A U.S. official noted that Iraq has decided not to distribute any food until 30 days worth of each of its "food basket" items is stocked in warehouses.
"They can't hand out a sandwich until there are 30 days supply....it is not logical and it is one of the things slowing down distribution," said the U.S. official.
The deal allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of its crude oil over six months, mainly to purchase food and medicine as an exception to broad sanctions instituted in August 1990, after Iraq invaded Kuwait.

The Security Council reviewed a 90-day progress report on the deal's implementation on Thursday. Although the oil sales side of the deal was proceeding with little trouble, the report said aid deliveries were slower than expected.

On Wednesday, the United States lifted its objections to 13 aid contracts for soap and detergent, only after gaining assurances the shipments would be sufficiently monitored by U.N. observers on the ground.
Earlier Thursday, France said first deliveries might not reach the Iraqi people until May, a timetable not disputed by a U.S. official.
"That's generally right, a week or two in either direction," said the U.S. official.
Iraqi decisions on the length of oil contracts and warehousing practices were singled out as delaying deliveries.
"Iraq decided on 30-day pricing contracts (for oil). Although that is industry practice, they could have had 10- or 15-day contracts," said a U.S. official.
The U.S. said once the so-called "start-up" problems were solved, then distribution should run smoothly.
Polish Ambassador Zbigniew Wlosowicz, president of the Security Council, said the program was complex, but hoped the implemtation would succeed with the continued cooperation of the Iraqi government.
